title: How can ten digits make a big multiple of five and a small even one?
description: The ten digits zero to nine are used once each to make a ten digit number. The biggest digits go first for the largest multiple of five, and the smallest start with a small fix at the end gives the smallest even number. Each number is checked at the end.
teaching_notes: One idea: the leftmost digits decide how big a number is, and the last digit decides whether it is a multiple of five or even. Watch for students who forget that the first digit cannot be zero.

source: Using all digits from 0-9 exactly once (the first digit cannot be 0) to create a 10-digit number, write the largest multiple of 5 and the smallest even number.
video_script.why: The child reads and compares large numbers, and now builds the largest and smallest numbers from digits using place value.
video_script.substitution: Put the biggest digits at the left for the largest number, the smallest allowed digits at the left for the smallest, and fix only the last digit to meet the rule.
video_script.anchor: ten digit cards, 0 to 9, in a row, with a ten digit number frame above them
video_script.payoff_line: Place the digits in order and fix only the last digits

final_answer.spoken: the largest multiple of five is nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one, zero, and the smallest even number is one, zero, two, three, four, five, six, seven, nine, eight

maths_rules: a multiple of 5 ends in 0 or 5; the largest uses the digits 9 down to 0, so 9876543210, which ends in 0
the smallest ten digit number with the digits 0 to 9 once is 1023456789, which ends in 9 and is odd
swapping the last two digits gives 1023456798, which ends in 8 and is even, and it is the next number up
checks: each of the digits 0 to 9 appears once in both numbers; neither starts with 0
video_script.design: One idea: place value picks the order of the digits; the last digit settles the rule. The ten digit cards stay in the anchor band; the working band builds each number. No hard clear.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, for the largest number, put the biggest digits at the left.
That gives nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one, zero.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>It ends in zero, so it is a multiple of five.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, for the smallest number, start with one, then zero, then the rest in rising order.
<bookmark mark='m1b'/>That gives one, zero, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>It ends in nine, which is odd.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Swap the last two digits, so the number ends in eight, which is even.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: check: each digit 0 to 9 is used once in both numbers; neither starts with 0; the swap changes only the last two digits

marks.m1: a tick appears for each digit used once in both numbers
marks.m2: a tick appears for the first digit not being 0
marks.m3: the last two digits are lit

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, check both numbers.
Each uses all ten digits once, and neither starts with zero.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The swap changes only the last two digits, so the number grows by the least it can.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>No other rearrangement ends in an even digit with a smaller number.
